newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - IBCA boosts Finland rating, EMU hopes high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - IBCA boosts Finland rating, EMU hopes high.

text.p: The Republic of Finland, bolstered by economic and fiscal improvements, received a credit rating upgrade from European rating agency IBCA.
Finland's long-term foreign currency rating was raised to AA plus from AA, and its local currency ratings were affirmed.

Finland, like many European countries, is working hard to make the grade for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), under which the euro is due to be introduced in 1999. Finland is widely considered in financial markets to be among the more likely candidates for early membership.
IBCA said Finland's case for early membership in a single European currency was strengthened by a helpful political and fundamental background.

"Finland's impressive resilience in the face of sharper economic shocks in the last recession than those faced by any other Western European country have demonstrated once again the country's remarkable social cohesion," IBCA said in a statement.
The agency noted that Finland already satisfies the Maastricht criteria, strengthening the belief it will be among the founding members of EMU.

Maastricht requires countries to have a budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product by the end of 1997, overall public debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP, and a degree of convergence in inflation and long-term interest rates.
Among the many benefits of EMU, it will lock in the lower real interest rates that have already been achieved, IBCA said.
It said these factors acted to offset the country's one enduring weakness, its continued overdependence on forestry.

"Even here progress has been made in moving upmarket from bulk pulp to higher quality paper and other products, as well as in developing electronics, services and other non-forest sectors," IBCA said.
As reasons for the rating upgrade, the agency cited the steady and significant progress made in most aspects of the economy.

"Finland's public finances are now sound. The public ratio has stabilised at a level below the Maastricht criterion. A further plus point is that fiscal adjustment has been achieved almost wholly on the expenditure side, with no significant tax increases," IBCA said.

But Finland still has to tackle with unemployment which although it has declined since 1994, has only done so at a slow rate as rapid productivity growth has dampened the demand for labour, IBCA said.
At the same time the rating agency confirmed Finland's A1 plus short-term foreign currency and AAA local currency sovereign ratings.
